B01:
RAG and fine-tuning solve different problems, and picking the wrong one is expensive to unwind. RAG pulls from a live knowledge base at query time, so answers stay current and the model can cite the exact document it drew from. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge and tone into the weights: faster responses, consistent style, no retrieval hop.

The tension gets concrete fast. Say you run a customer-support knowledge base of 100,000 documents. Retrieve from it, fine-tune on it, or both? The answer turns on how often the content changes, whether users need to see sources, and what latency they'll tolerate.

This post works through that decision.
B02:
Every index you add to a Postgres table taxes every write to it. Each INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE has to maintain every index on the table — including the ones no query ever uses. Unused indexes are pure cost: bloated writes, inflated storage, slower vacuum cycles, nothing in return.

A recent client made the point better than any benchmark could. One of their core tables had accumulated 23 indexes over the years. We audited them and dropped 14. Write throughput doubled — no hardware changes, no query rewrites, just less wasted work on every write.

Below: the indexing pitfalls we see most often, how to find unused indexes in your own database, and a checklist for keeping them lean.
B03:
Every company claims to have remote onboarding figured out, right up until a new hire spends their first week waiting for access and guessing who to ask for help. On a distributed team those frictions compound, because nobody walks past your desk and notices you're stuck.

We onboarded 27 remote hires in the past year and got plenty wrong before we got it right. The number we track is time-to-first-PR, and it fell from 12 days to 5. New engineers now ship real code in their first week instead of their third.

This guide is the playbook that got us there: how we structure day one, what the onboarding buddy actually does, which documentation earned its keep and which didn't, and the metrics we watch to keep improving.

We surveyed 412 designers for The State of Design Systems 2026, across industries, company sizes, and levels of design maturity. One finding frames everything else: 61% say their design system is partially adopted at best. Most teams have built the system. Far fewer have made it the source of truth it was meant to be.

The stalls have familiar causes — unclear ownership, competing priorities, drift between design and code, documentation that lags the components it describes. But the data also shows what working adoption looks like, and the teams that get there share habits consistent enough to copy.

This report unpacks the numbers and pulls out the practices worth taking back to your own team.

Nobody brags about their savings account at parties. An emergency fund has no compounding chart to admire, no dopamine hit — and it's still the financial move that pays off most reliably.

The standard advice is 3–6 months of expenses: enough cushion to absorb a job loss, a medical bill, or a surprise car repair without reaching for a credit card. Simple to say. Genuinely hard to do on a normal paycheck.

It took me 14 months to build mine on a $52k salary, and the hard part was never the math. It was the habits — the trade-offs, and staying motivated through months when the balance barely seemed to move.

Here's how I did it: the budget changes that mattered most, the automation that kept me consistent, and what I'd tell anyone who has started and stalled.

The average mid-market company runs purchasing across 7 different tools: spreadsheets, email threads, an ERP module, a standalone approval app or two. Each tool made sense when someone added it. Together they make a process nobody can see end to end — requests stall between systems, approvers don't know what's waiting on them, and finance loses track of committed spend until the invoice lands.

The fix is consolidation: requests, approvals, and vendor management in one workflow. Companies that make the switch have seen 14-day approval cycles drop to 3.

This post covers how procurement tooling got this fragmented, what a consolidated setup looks like in practice, and how to tell whether your organization is ready to change it.
B08:
On Tuesday we had a 4-hour outage. The cause was an expired TLS certificate on an internal service that sat in the request path — a service most of us rarely thought about, with a certificate nobody realized was near expiry. It lapsed quietly and took a surprising amount of the stack down with it.

The failure mode made diagnosis slow. Alerts fired, but the errors cascaded in ways that pointed everywhere except the certificate, and tracing them back to the source took longer than it should have.

This postmortem walks through the full timeline and contributing factors, plus the three things we're changing: automated certificate-expiry monitoring across all services, documented rotation runbooks for every internal certificate, and game-day testing of certificate failure modes.

If you run internal services over TLS, check your expiry dates today. We thought we'd have noticed too.

T01:
Last year I sent thousands of cold emails and got an 8% reply rate.

Cold email isn't dead. Most of it is just bad in fixable ways.

5 lessons: 🧵

1/ Keep it to 4 lines. Your prospect is scanning on a phone between meetings — four lines is enough to say who you are, why you're relevant, and what you want. Anything longer gets archived unread.

2/ One CTA. Not two, not three. Every extra ask cuts your reply rate. "Worth a 15-min chat?" beats a menu of options every time.

3/ Personalize the first line, but only if it's real. "Loved your post on X" works exactly once — when you actually read the post. One genuine sentence beats five templated ones.

4/ Follow up. Most replies come from the 2nd or 3rd email, not the 1st. A polite bump isn't annoying; it's how deals happen. Silence is not a no.

5/ Track everything — subject lines, send times, CTAs — and iterate weekly. The 8% didn't come from a magic template. It came from treating cold email as a system, not a lottery.
T02:
Most meetings should be memos.

Writing forces clarity, respects everyone's time, and leaves a record you can search. If an idea can't survive being written down, it won't survive a 60-minute meeting either.
T03:
19 months ago I launched a $49 one-time product.

This week we crossed $10k MRR — no funding, no team, no audience.

What actually worked, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ Start ugly. V1 was a $49 one-time purchase: no subscriptions, no dashboard, barely a landing page. It made a handful of sales — and proved people would pay. Validation first, polish later.

2/ Listen for the pivot. Customers kept coming back with the same recurring problem, and a one-time product couldn't serve it. Month 7: switched to subscriptions. Revenue dipped for a few weeks, then compounded.

3/ Do things that don't scale. I onboarded every early customer myself, answered every support email, and asked every churned user why they left. Those conversations wrote the roadmap.

4/ 19 months to $10k MRR is not a rocket ship. That's the point — slow, profitable, compounding growth you fully own. If you're bootstrapping: the boring months count.

T05:
Can LLMs judge other LLMs?

A new paper tests LLM-as-judge against human evaluators. The answer: yes for routine work, no for creative work — and the gap is wide.

The findings, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ Overall, LLM judges agree with human evaluators 81% of the time. For routine evaluation tasks, that makes an LLM judge a reasonable stand-in for a human rater.

2/ On creative tasks, agreement drops to 64%. Where there's no objectively correct answer — style, originality, taste — LLM judges and humans stop seeing the same quality.

3/ The likely reason: judges reward surface features like structure, fluency, and length. LLM judges like writing that looks good more than writing that is good.

4/ So use LLM-as-judge for scale on objective tasks, and keep humans on creative work. 81% is not 100%, and 64% is uncomfortably close to a coin flip.

R01: Automated code review promises lower defect rates and reduced reviewer workload, but existing tools remain narrow in scope and imprecise. We present ReviewBot, an automated code-review system that combines static analysis with learned models to surface defects within the pull-request workflow. Evaluated on 1,200 pull requests from 8 repositories spanning multiple languages and project sizes, ReviewBot caught 34% more defects than baseline linters at a 12% false-positive rate, which developers in our study rated acceptable for day-to-day use. Its largest gains come on cross-file inconsistencies and API-misuse patterns that traditional linters routinely miss. We discuss deployment considerations — reviewer trust, alert fatigue, and integration with existing continuous-integration pipelines — and conclude that automated review can augment, though not replace, human reviewers. Future work includes adaptive precision thresholds and repository-specific tuning; we release our evaluation framework to support reproducibility.
R02:
We surveyed 156 enterprises across industries and regions about their data-governance practices, challenges, and priorities. The central finding: 44% have no data-classification policy. Without classification, an organization cannot say consistently which data is sensitive, regulated, or business-critical, and every downstream control — access management, retention, encryption, incident response — rests on guesswork rather than policy.

The costs show up in practice. Organizations without foundational governance report longer audit cycles, higher breach-response costs, and growing friction as AI initiatives demand well-understood, well-labeled data.

To close the gap, this whitepaper recommends a 5-step maturity model that takes organizations from initial data discovery through classification, ownership, policy enforcement, and continuous monitoring, with concrete milestones and self-assessment criteria at each step.

Data governance has become a prerequisite for compliance, security, and AI readiness. Enterprises that close the classification gap first will move faster, and more safely, than those that wait.
R03:
At pilot firms using AI-assisted contract review, review time is down 60%. Work that consumed days of associate attention now takes hours, and legal ops leaders under pressure to do more with less have noticed.

The caveat matters as much as the number: hallucinated citations. AI tools can produce authorities that look entirely plausible and do not exist, and courts have shown little patience with filings that contain them. Every AI-assisted output needs qualified human review before it goes anywhere. No exceptions.

The guardrails are forming, too. The ABA has issued guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI, centered on competence, confidentiality, and supervision. Adopt the technology; own the output.

For legal teams starting now: begin with high-volume, lower-risk workflows like contract review, measure everything, and keep lawyers firmly in the loop. The firms that pair AI's speed with legal judgment will set the standard for what legal service costs — and what it looks like.

If your team has run one of these pilots, I'd like to hear what your numbers looked like.
